terminal.description: A shell that starts in the shop's top folder. Read a file before you save anything from it.

tasks.title: Join the two sign-up lists
tasks.description:
Idris keeps two lists of email addresses in `mailing`: `market-signups.txt` from the market stall and `shop-signups.txt` from the shop. Make one list, `mailing-list.txt` in the top folder, with every line of the market list first and every line of the shop list under it.

Check compares `mailing-list.txt` line by line with the two lists, in that order.
nextSteps: Look at both lists with `cat` or `less`.
Print both of them with one command, the market list first.
Run that command again with `>` and the new file's name after it.
Look at `mailing-list.txt` with `less`, and press `q` to leave.
hints: The lesson's part on `cat` says what it does when it gets more than one file name.
`cat` prints the files you name one after the other. `>` keeps all of it in one file, as long as it is one command.
Run `cat mailing/market-signups.txt mailing/shop-signups.txt > mailing-list.txt` from the top folder.

tasks.title: Save the start of the order list
tasks.description:
The accountant wants the header line of `sales/web-orders.csv` and the ten orders under it, nothing more. Save those first lines into `first-orders.txt` in the top folder.

Check compares `first-orders.txt` with the first lines of `sales/web-orders.csv`: the header, then ten orders.
nextSteps: Look at the start of `sales/web-orders.csv` without printing all of it.
Count the lines you need: the header is a line too.
Ask for that many lines, and save them with `>`.
hints: One command from the lesson prints only the start of a file.
`head` prints 10 lines unless `-n` asks for another number. The header and ten orders are more than 10 lines.
Run `head -n 11 sales/web-orders.csv > first-orders.txt` from the top folder.

tasks.title: Save the last entries of the March log
tasks.description:
Press 2 stopped on Tuesday 31 March. Hesper wants the last 8 entries of `logs/press-mar.log`, the lines at the very end, saved into `last-entries.txt` in the top folder.

Check compares `last-entries.txt` with the last 8 lines of the March log.
nextSteps: Open `logs/press-mar.log` with `less` to see how long it is, then press `q`.
Ask for 8 lines, and save them with `>`.
hints: The newest entries of a log are at the bottom. One command prints the bottom of a file.
`tail` prints the last 10 lines, and `-n` sets another number.
Run `tail -n 8 logs/press-mar.log > last-entries.txt` from the top folder.

less: read a file one screen at a time

tasks.title: Count the entries in each log
tasks.description:
Each line of a press log is one entry. Idris wants to know how many lines each month's log has. Count the lines of every `.log` file in `logs` in one command, and save what it prints into `entry-counts.txt` in the top folder. `logs` also holds `README.txt`, which is not a log.

Check reads each count in `entry-counts.txt` and compares it with the number of lines in that log. The `total` line may be there or not.
nextSteps: Run `ls logs` and see which files are logs.
Count the lines of one log first.
Count every log in one command, with a pattern like the ones in the issue on many files at once.
Save that with `>`, and look at `entry-counts.txt`.
hints: The lesson's counting command takes an option that counts lines and nothing else.
`wc -l` takes several files, or a pattern that matches only the logs, and prints one line per file.
Run `wc -l logs/*.log > entry-counts.txt` from the top folder.
